# Introduction

`cfomics` estimates conditional average treatment effects (CATE) for
high-dimensional omics data (many genes, few samples). Many CATE estimators
exist and no single one is reliably best in advance: the winner depends on the
data. `cfomics` therefore provides one interface to **compare** estimators on a
data-only loss, **select** one, or **combine** them into an ensemble, and to
carry the resulting individual effects into standard Bioconductor analyses.

This vignette walks through that workflow on a small simulated
`SummarizedExperiment`. The data are synthetic and used only to make the steps
runnable end to end.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("cfomics")
```

```{r libs, message = FALSE}
library(cfomics)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
```

The estimators wrapped by `econml`/`catenets` (the meta-learners and neural
methods) run in a Python environment that `basilisk` builds at install time.
The R-native `grf` step below always runs; the rest of the workflow runs when
that environment is available.

```{r haspy}
has_py <- requireNamespace("basilisk", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("reticulate", quietly = TRUE)
```

# Example data

`cf_example_data()` returns a `SummarizedExperiment` of raw RNA-seq counts with
a randomised treatment, a continuous outcome, two clinical covariates
(`age`, `sex`) and a planted heterogeneous treatment effect. The true
individual effect is stored in `colData` and the signal genes are flagged in
`rowData` (so you can experiment against a known ground truth).

```{r data}
se <- cf_example_data(n = 150, p = 600, seed = 1)
se
colData(se)[1:3, ]
```

# A single estimator

`cf_fit()` fits one method. `grf` (causal forest) is R-native and needs no
Python. The result carries the average effect and, for CATE-capable methods,
one estimate per sample.

```{r grf}
fit <- cf_fit(data = se, Y = "outcome", T = "treatment",
              X_baseline = c("age", "sex"),
              method = "grf", n_features = 300)
fit
head(predict(fit, type = "tau"))
```

# Comparing estimators

`cf_compare()` fits several methods with cross-fitting (`partition = "oof"`)
and ranks them by a data-only CATE loss (`r_loss`/`dr_loss`). The evaluation
nuisance models are fit by an independent learner (`eval_nuisance = "xgboost"`),
so the score does not favour any compared method; here the propensity is known
(a randomised trial), so we pass it directly.

```{r compare, eval = has_py}
methods <- c("grf", "tlearner", "xlearner")
cmp <- cf_compare(data = se, Y = "outcome", T = "treatment",
                  X_baseline = c("age", "sex"),
                  methods = methods,
                  n_features = 300, model_outcome = "lasso",
                  eval_nuisance = "xgboost", propensity_score = 0.5,
                  random_state = 1)
cmp
```

The scoreboard is the basis for choosing a method; a lower loss is better.
Neural-network methods (`tarnet`, `dragonnet`, `cevae`, `ganite`) can be added
to `methods` in the same call when compute allows.

The best base learner is also data-dependent. `base_learners` compares the
meta / DR learners (`slearner`, `tlearner`, `xlearner`, `drlearner`) across
their base learners in one call: each is expanded to one row per base learner
(labelled `method_base`, e.g. `xlearner_rf`), while `grf` / `bcf` / NN methods
stay single. The propensity and evaluation nuisance are held fixed across the
grid, so only the outcome / CATE learner varies.

```{r compare-base, eval = FALSE}
cmp_grid <- cf_compare(data = se, Y = "outcome", T = "treatment",
                       X_baseline = c("age", "sex"),
                       methods = c("grf", "xlearner", "drlearner"),
                       base_learners = c("elastic_net", "rf"),
                       n_features = 300, eval_nuisance = "xgboost",
                       propensity_score = 0.5, random_state = 1)
cmp_grid$scoreboard[, c("label", "method", "base", "r_loss", "rank")]
```

# How much do methods agree?

`cf_model_stability()` reports how similarly the methods rank patients by
benefit. Low agreement is a signal that the choice of method matters for this
dataset.

```{r stability, eval = has_py}
cf_model_stability(cmp)
```

# Selecting or combining

`cf_select()` returns the lowest-loss method. `cf_ensemble()` instead combines
the per-patient effects across methods; `r_stacking` weights them by fit, which
protects against a single poor choice.

```{r select-ensemble, eval = has_py}
sel <- cf_select(cmp)
sel$selection_stats$selected_method

ens <- cf_ensemble(cmp, method = "r_stacking")
```

# Evaluating a chosen model

`cf_evaluate()` measures how well a model prioritises patients (rank-weighted
average treatment effect and grouped effects), again with an independent
nuisance and the known propensity.

```{r evaluate, eval = has_py}
winner <- cmp$models[[sel$selection_stats$selected_method]]
cf_evaluate(winner, eval_nuisance = "xgboost", eval_propensity_score = 0.5)
```

# Which genes drive the effect?

`cf_interpret()` distils a fitted model (or the ensemble) into a surrogate
SHAP explanation: an importance and a direction per gene. We use the ensemble
effect here.

```{r interpret, eval = has_py}
itp <- cf_interpret(ens)
# `vi` is keyed by surrogate; each holds a per-gene importance/direction table.
head(itp$vi$ridge$features)
```

# Benefit groups and a treatment rule

`cf_benefit_groups()` splits patients into high- and low-benefit groups from the
(out-of-fold) estimated effects, and `cf_rule()` builds a simple
treat/don't-treat rule.

```{r groups, eval = has_py}
grp <- cf_benefit_groups(ens)
grp$n_per_group
```

# Connecting to Bioconductor: a biology-bridge recipe

The workflow's output lives naturally on the `SummarizedExperiment`. Write the
estimated effect and benefit group back with `cf_attach_results()`, then use
standard Bioconductor tools to describe the biology of the benefit groups.

```{r attach, eval = has_py}
se <- cf_attach_results(se, ens, what = "all", groups = grp)
colData(se)[1:3, c("cf_tau", "cf_group")]
```

**Differential expression between benefit groups** with `limma`/`edgeR`:

```{r deg, eval = has_py && requireNamespace("limma", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("edgeR", quietly = TRUE)}
library(edgeR); library(limma)
grp_f  <- factor(colData(se)$cf_group)
dge    <- DGEList(assay(se, "counts"))
dge    <- dge[filterByExpr(dge, group = grp_f), , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
dge    <- normLibSizes(dge)
design <- model.matrix(~ grp_f)
efit   <- eBayes(lmFit(voom(dge, design), design))
topTable(efit, coef = 2, number = 5)[, c("logFC", "adj.P.Val")]
```

**Pathway activity related to the estimated benefit** with `GSVA` ssGSEA
scores correlated against the individual effect (`cf_tau`):

```{r gsva, eval = has_py && requireNamespace("GSVA", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("msigdbr", quietly = TRUE)}
library(GSVA); library(msigdbr)
h    <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H")
sets <- split(h$gene_symbol, h$gs_name)
logcpm <- edgeR::cpm(assay(se, "counts"), log = TRUE)
scores <- gsva(ssgseaParam(logcpm, sets), verbose = FALSE)
tau    <- colData(se)$cf_tau
cors   <- sort(apply(scores, 1, cor, tau, method = "spearman"), decreasing = TRUE)
head(cors, 3)
```

These descriptions are exploratory: the groups and scores derive from the
estimated effect, so treat the associations as hypothesis-generating.
